# Problem 1  NY NOAA Weather Data

## Import and describe the dataset
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
names(ny_noaa)
dim(ny_noaa)
str(ny_noaa)
head(ny_noaa,50)
```


```{r}
ny_noaa|>
summarize(
  missing_snow=sum(is.na(snow)),
  missing_prcp=sum(is.na(prcp)),
  missing_snwd=sum(is.na(snwd)),
  missing_tmax=sum(is.na(tmax)),
  missing_tmin=sum(is.na(tmin))
)
```

Description: This dataset has 7 variables and 2,595,176 observations. Each observation represents a weather record from a specific weather station on a particular date. 

In these variables, " Weather station ID(id), maximum temperature(tmax), minimum temperature(tmin)" are character variables, "(date)" is a date variable, "precipitation(prcp), snowfall(snow), snow depth(snwd)" are integer variables. 

In all these observations, "snow" has 381,221 missing values, "prcp" has 145,838 missing values, "snwd" has 591,786 missing values, "tmax" has 1,134,358 missing values, "tmin" has 1,134,420 missing values.

## Create separate variables for year, month, and day
```{r}
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date)
  )
names(ny_noaa)
dim(ny_noaa)
head(ny_noaa,50)
```

## Ensure observations are given in reasonable units. 
```{r}
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
str(ny_noaa)
tail(ny_noaa,100)
```

## For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? Why?
```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  filter(!is.na(snow))|>
  count(snow, sort= TRUE) |>
  head(n=10)
```

The most commonly observed snowfall value was 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations, because most days had no snowfall. Other common values included 25 mm, 13 mm, 51 mm, and 76 mm. These values correspond to common snowfall measurements in inches(25 mm=1 inch), which may reflect conversion from inches to millimeters in dataset description.

## Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years. Is there any observable / interpretable structure? Any outliers?

```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  filter (month %in% c(1,7),!is.na(tmax)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax)
    ) |>
ggplot(aes(x=year, y=mean_tmax, group=id)) +
  geom_line(alpha=0.3) +
  facet_grid(.~month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature Across Years",
    x= "Year",
    y= "Mean Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

The two-panel plot shows that average maximum temperatures in July are substantially higher than those in January across weather stations. Both months show considerable year-to-year variation, with no clear consistent long-term trend. Most weather stations follow similar temperature patterns, although some variation exists between stations.

A potential outlier is observed in July around 1988, where one station has an unusually low average maximum temperature of approximately 14°C. Some unusually low temperatures are also observed in January. These observations may represent outliers, but further examination would be needed to determine whether they are genuine measurements or data errors.

## Make a two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset (note that a scatterplot may not be the best option); and (ii) make a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.
```{r}
temp_plot = ny_noaa |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax),!is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=tmin,y=tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum Temperature vs Minumum Temperature",
    x = " Minumum Temperature(°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature(°C)"
  )+
    theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
snow_plot = ny_noaa |>
  filter(snow>0,snow<100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=factor(year),y=snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall(mm)"
  )+
    theme_minimal() +
scale_x_discrete(
  breaks = c("1985", "1990", "1995",
             "2000", "2005", "2010")
)
```

```{r}
library(patchwork)
temp_plot + snow_plot
```

The first plot shows a positive relationship between minimum and maximum temperatures. Most observations are concentrated along an upward trend, although there are some possible outliers.

The second plot shows that snowfall distributions are similar across most years, with a median of around 25 mm. A few years have slightly different distributions and some possible outliers.




# Problem 2  Accelerometer Data

## Import and Inspect dataset
```{r}
library(readr)
covar_df=read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv")
accel_df=read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv")

dim(covar_df)
dim(accel_df)
names(covar_df)
```

## Recode the covar dataset
```{r}
covar_df=read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv",
                  skip = 5,
                  col_names=c("SEQN","sex","age","BMI","education")
                  )
dim(covar_df)
names(covar_df)
str(covar_df)
```

## Data Cleaning (covar_df)
```{r}
colSums(is.na(covar_df))
```

```{r}
covar_df=covar_df |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI),
         !is.na(education),
         age>=21
  )
dim(covar_df)
colSums(is.na(covar_df))
```

## Convert categorical variables(covar_df)
```{r}
covar_df=covar_df |>
  mutate(
    sex=factor(sex,
           levels=c(1,2),
           labels=c("male","female")
    )
    ,
    education=factor(education,
           levels=c(1,2,3),
           labels=c("Less than high school","High school equivalent","More than high school"),
           ordered= TRUE
    )
  )

str(covar_df)
table(covar_df$sex)
table(covar_df$education)
head(covar_df,10)
```

## Merge the datasets
```{r}
nhanes_df = covar_df |>
  left_join(accel_df, by="SEQN")
dim(nhanes_df)
```

## Make a demographic summary table
Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category, and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category. Comment on these items.
```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  count(sex,education)
```

```{r}
demo_table = nhanes_df |>
  count(education,sex) |>
pivot_wider(
  names_from=sex,
    values_from=n
)
demo_table
```

```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=age,color=sex))+
  geom_density()+
  facet_wrap(~education)+
  labs(
    title="Age Distribution by Sex and Education",
    x="Age",
    y="Density",
    color="Sex"
  )
```

Age distributions varied across education categories. Participants with less than a high school education tended to be older, while those with more than a high school education had higher age densities among younger adults. In the high school equivalent group, female participants tended to be older than male participants.

## Total Activity Analysis
Traditional analyses of accelerometer data focus on the total activity over the day. Using your tidied dataset, aggregate across minutes to create a total activity variable for each participant. Plot these total activities (y-axis) against age (x-axis); your plot should compare men to women and have separate panels for each education level. Include a trend line or a smooth to illustrate differences. Comment on your plot.

```{r}
nhanes_df=nhanes_df |>
  mutate(
    total_activity=rowSums(
      pick(starts_with("min"))
    )
  )
dim(nhanes_df)
```

```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x=age,y=total_activity,color=sex))+
  geom_point(alpha=0.5)+
  geom_smooth()+
facet_wrap(~education)+
  labs(
    title="Association of total Activity and age",
    x="Age(years)",
    y="Total Daily Activity(sum of MIMS)",
    color="sex"
    )
```

Total daily activity generally decreased with increasing age, although the trends were not strictly linear. In the high school equivalent and more than high school education groups, females tended to have higher total daily activity than males across most ages. In the less than high school education group, females generally had higher activity at younger ages, while males tended to have higher activity after approximately age 50.

## 24-hour Activity Patterns
Accelerometer data allows the inspection activity over the course of the day. Make a three-panel plot that shows the 24-hour activity time courses for each education level and use color to indicate sex. Describe in words any patterns or conclusions you can make based on this graph; including smooth trends may help identify differences.
```{r}
nhanes_long=nhanes_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("min"),
    names_to="minute",
      values_to="activity"
  )
dim(nhanes_long)
str(nhanes_long)
```

```{r}
nhanes_long = nhanes_long |>
  mutate(
    minute = parse_number(minute)
  )
str(nhanes_long)
```

```{r}
nhanes_long |>
group_by(minute,sex,education) |>
  summarize(mean_activity=mean(activity))|>
  ggplot(aes(x=minute,y=mean_activity,color=sex))+
  geom_line(alpha=0.5)+
  facet_wrap(~education)+
  labs(
    title="24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education",
    x="Time(mins)",
    y="Mean Activity",
    color="Sex"
  )
```

Overall, activity levels were higher during the day and lower at night. Females generally had higher daytime activity levels than males, especially in the more than high school education group. Participants with less than a high school education tended to have relatively higher daytime activity levels than those in the high school equivalent group.





# Problem 3  Citi Bike Data

## Import and check the dataset
```{r}
library(readr)
Jan_2020_Citi <- read_csv("data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv")
Jan_2024_Citi <- read_csv("data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv")
July_2020_Citi <- read_csv("data/July 2020 Citi.csv")
July_2024_Citi <- read_csv("data/July 2024 Citi.csv")
dim(Jan_2020_Citi)
dim(Jan_2024_Citi)
dim(July_2020_Citi)
dim(July_2024_Citi)
str(Jan_2020_Citi)
str(Jan_2024_Citi)
str(July_2020_Citi)
str(July_2024_Citi)
```

## Merge four datasets first
```{r}
Jan_2020_Citi=Jan_2020_Citi |>
  mutate(
    source = "Jan_2020"
  )
Jan_2024_Citi=Jan_2024_Citi |>
  mutate(
    source = "Jan_2024"
  )
July_2020_Citi=July_2020_Citi |>
  mutate(
    source = "July_2020"
  )
July_2024_Citi=July_2024_Citi |>
  mutate(
    source = "July_2024"
  )
```

```{r}
citi_df = bind_rows(
  Jan_2020_Citi,
  Jan_2024_Citi,
  July_2020_Citi,
  July_2024_Citi
)

str(citi_df)
dim(citi_df)
count(citi_df, source)
head(citi_df)
```
The final combined dataset contains 99,485 observations and 9 variables, covering January and July of 2020 and 2024. Each original dataset represents a 1% sample of Citi Bike rides lasting less than four hours. The combined dataset includes information on ride duration, weekdays, bike type, membership status, starting and ending stations, as well as the newly created year and month variables.

## Build new variables----year & month
```{r}
citi_df=citi_df |>
  separate(
    col=source,
    into=c("month","year"),
    sep="_",
    convert= TRUE
  )
str(citi_df)
count(citi_df,month,year)
```

## Number of rides by membership status
Produce a reader-friendly table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members. Comment on these results.

```{r}
demo_table = citi_df |>
  count(year,month,member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from=member_casual ,
    values_from=n
  )
  demo_table
```

Across all four periods, the number of rides taken by members was consistently higher than that taken by casual riders. For both groups, the number of rides was higher in July than in January. Additionally, ride counts were higher in 2024 than in 2020 for both months and both membership groups.

## A table shows the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024
Make a table showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024; include the number of rides originating from these stations.

```{r}
top5_stations = citi_df |>
  filter(year==2024,month=="July") |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
head(n=5)

top5_stations
```

Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers was the most popular starting station in July 2024, with 163 rides in the sample. The number of rides was relatively similar across the top five stations, ranging from 146 to 163.

## Median Ride Duration
Make a plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. This plot can include one or more panels, but should facilitate comparison across all variables of interest. Comment on your observations from this plot.

```{r}
citi_df |>
  mutate(
    weekdays=factor(weekdays,levels =c(
      "Monday","Tuesday","Wednesday","Thursday","Friday","Saturday","Sunday"),
    labels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu",
           "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"))
  ) |>
  group_by(month,year,weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_ride_duration=median(duration)) |>
      ggplot(aes(x=weekdays,y=median_ride_duration,group=1))+
      geom_line(alpha=0.5)+
  labs(x="weekdays",
       y="median ride duration",
    title="Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year")+
  facet_wrap(year ~ month)
```

Median ride duration was generally higher in July than in January. Rides in 2020 also tended to have longer median durations than those in 2024, particularly in July. Weekend rides, especially on Saturdays, generally had longer median durations than weekday rides.

## Ride Duration Distribution
There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.

```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year==2024) |>
  ggplot(aes( x=duration,color=rideable_type))+
  geom_density()+
  facet_grid(month~member_casual)+
  labs(
    x="Ride Duration(Minutes)",
    y="Density",
  title="Ride Duration Distribution by month, membership status and bike type."
  )
```

Ride duration distributions were strongly right-skewed across all groups. Member rides were more concentrated at shorter durations compared with casual rides. Classic and electric bikes showed broadly similar, highly overlapping distributions, although their density peaks varied across groups. The distributions also appeared slightly more spread out in July than in January, particularly among casual riders.
